string.text: {=balkan_culture_bosniaken_desc}The Eyalet of Bosnia is the Ottoman bulwark on the Habsburg and Venetian frontier. Its captaincies, the kapetanije, guard the river crossings and mountain passes, manned by azaps and musketeers who know every ford. The sipahis hold their timars in return for service on horseback, and the reckless deli horsemen ride ahead of every raid.

{=balkan_culture_bulgaren_desc}For three centuries, since 1396, the Bulgarians have lived under the Sultan. Some serve the empire as voynuks or as guards of roads and mountain passes and are freed from taxes in return. Others have taken to the forests as hajduks. The uprising of Chiprovtsi in 1688, led by Catholic Bulgarians, was crushed and the town destroyed.

{=balkan_culture_deutsche_desc}German settlers came to the frontier lands of Styria, Carniola and the reconquered plains as farmers, craftsmen and soldiers. The imperial regiments recruit their pikemen and musketeers among them, and the heavy cuirassiers of the Emperor are drawn from their nobility.

{=balkan_culture_griechen_desc}The Greeks of Macedonia, Thessaly and the islands live under the Sultan as his Orthodox subjects. Greek ship owners carry much of the empire's trade by sea, and Phanariot families in Constantinople serve the Porte as dragomans, its interpreters. In the villages the kodjabashis speak for the community and collect the taxes. In the mountains the armatoles guard the passes on behalf of the Ottomans, while the klephts live as brigands; many armatoles were klephts before.

{=balkan_culture_kroaten_desc}Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia call themselves a kingdom of their own, joined to the Habsburg crown. Since the 16th century the Military Frontier has held the border against the Ottomans: its settlers receive land, freedom of religion and lower taxes, and in exchange they must fight for the Empire. Their nobles still ride as armoured cavalry, while the border men fight with sabre and arquebus.

{=balkan_culture_ragusaner_desc}The Republic of Ragusa keeps its freedom with gold rather than steel. It has paid tribute to the Sultan since 1458, and its ships sail under its own flag. Behind the great walls of the city a small guard of halberdiers and arquebusiers serves the Rector, who holds office for only one month so that no man may rule alone.

{=balkan_culture_serben_desc}In 1690 Patriarch Arsenije III led more than 30,000 Serbs out of Belgrade into the Habsburg lands, and Emperor Leopold I granted them privileges. Like the other settlers of the Military Frontier, they receive land, freedom of religion and lower taxes, and in exchange they defend the border. Others stayed under the Sultan.

{=balkan_culture_tuerken_desc}Turkish settlers, officials and soldiers have lived in the Balkan towns since the conquest. The Janissaries, the Sultan's standing infantry, are the most famous musketeers of the empire, while the sipahis hold their land in return for service on horseback.

{=balkan_culture_ungarn_desc}After a century and a half of war the Hungarian plains are slowly filling with people again. The hajdús, irregular foot soldiers, fight with musket and sabre, and the light hussars have become famous in every army of Europe.

{=balkan_culture_venezianer_desc}The Most Serene Republic of Venice rules the Adriatic from its lagoon. Along the Dalmatian coast its provveditori govern walled ports filled with merchants, sailors and soldiers. Italian pikemen and musketeers hold the walls, the Oltremarini infantry of Dalmatian schiavoni and Albanians serves overseas, and the light cappelletti horsemen, Dalmatian Croats, ride in the hinterland.
